content: This is the second update of a Cochrane Review, originally published in 2013 and last updated in 2017. Laparoscopic surgery is now a widely adopted technique for managing various abdominal conditions. To create pneumoperitoneum, carbon dioxide is the most commonly used gas. While carbon dioxide fulfills most of the requirements for this purpose, its absorption into the body can lead to adverse effects. Consequently, alternative gases such as helium, argon, nitrogen, nitrous oxide, and room air have been proposed for use in pneumoperitoneum. The objective of this review was to evaluate the safety, advantages, and disadvantages of different gases used for pneumoperitoneum in patients undergoing laparoscopic abdominal or gynecological pelvic surgery. A comprehensive search was conducted on October 15, 2021, across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, and Ovid Embase, as well as three trial registries. Additional studies were identified through reference checking, citation searching, and direct contact with study authors. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared different gases for pneumoperitoneum in patients of any age, sex, or race undergoing laparoscopic abdominal or gynecological pelvic surgery under general anesthesia. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were employed for data collection and analysis. A total of 10 RCTs involving 583 participants were included. These trials compared nitrous oxide (four trials), helium (five trials), or room air (one trial) to carbon dioxide for pneumoperitoneum. All studies were single-center trials conducted in various countries, including the USA, Australia, China, Finland, Iran, and the Netherlands. The mean age of participants ranged from 27.6 to 49.0 years. Four trials compared nitrous oxide pneumoperitoneum (132 participants) to carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum (128 participants). None of these trials were at low risk of bias. The evidence regarding the effects of nitrous oxide compared to carbon dioxide on cardiopulmonary complications was highly uncertain (Peto odds ratio [OR] 2.62, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.78 to 8.85; 3 studies, 204 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, the evidence on surgical morbidity was also very uncertain (Peto OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.14 to 7.31; 3 studies, 207 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No serious adverse events were reported for either gas (4 studies, 260 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Four trials compared helium pneumoperitoneum (69 participants) to carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum (75 participants), with one additional trial involving 33 participants not specifying group allocation. None of these trials were at low risk of bias. The evidence on the effects of helium compared to carbon dioxide on cardiopulmonary complications was very uncertain (Peto OR 1.66, 95% CI 0.28 to 9.72; 3 studies, 128 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, the evidence on surgical morbidity was very uncertain (5 studies, 177 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Three cases of subcutaneous emphysema, a serious adverse event, were reported in the helium group (3 studies, 128 participants; very low-certainty evidence). One trial compared room air pneumoperitoneum (70 participants) to carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum (76 participants). This trial was at high risk of bias. No cardiopulmonary complications, serious adverse events, or deaths were observed in either group. In conclusion, the evidence is highly uncertain regarding the effects of nitrous oxide, helium, and room air compared to carbon dioxide on primary outcomes such as cardiopulmonary complications, surgical morbidity, and serious adverse events. The safety of these alternative gases remains unestablished, particularly in patients with high anesthetic risk.
